newsitem.title: USA: Key Congressman says U.S. budget deal near.
newsitem.headline: Key Congressman says U.S. budget deal near.

text.p: The Clinton Administration and congressional Republicans were close to a pact to balance the budget by 2002 but Medicare cost reduction and details of tax cuts were still an obstacle, a key Democrat said on Thursday.

"The big parameters are about to be settled I think. The devil however still is in the details and that's particularly true of tax cuts," said Representative John Spratt of South Carolina, a ranking Democrat on the House of Representatives Budget Committee.

"The White House and the Republican leadership were negotiating to late last night trying to reach final agreement and there's still some disagreement on the net amount of Medicare cost reduction and on the net tax cuts but they're within striking distance," Spratt told CNN television news.
President Bill Clinton also hinted that the broad outlines of a balanced budget agreement may be taking shape, and jokingly suggested using his crutches to beat the negotiators into making a deal.
Told about Spratt's comments on the budget, the president said: "Spratt's a smart man."

When informed that Spratt had said Medicare and taxes were sticking points in the negotiations, Clinton said: "I don't know. I'd have to get a report. Yesterday afternoon I wouldn't have said that, so I'd have to get a report."
Asked if there might be a budget deal on Thursday, he said: "(I'm going to) go to work and see."
One of the major hurdles the White House and Republicans face in their quest to win passage of the budget is the lack of support from House Democrats who have objected to deep domestic spending cuts.
Spratt said the net tax cut would be around $80 billion to $90 billion over five years as the agreement now stood, including a capital gains tax cut, estate tax relief and a child tax credit.
Spratt said Democrats in particular wanted to see details on a capital gains tax cut and estate tax relief.
The Republican chairmen of the congressional tax-writing committees have said they want discretion to craft the specifics of a tax bill within broad budget parameters.
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, spoke with Clinton late on Wednesday. The positions on tax cuts appeared to have narrowed.
Budget talks were to continue on Thursday. Clinton has said he hoped to conclude an agreement before leaving on Monday for Mexico.

The two sides have been negotiating for weeks on a plan to wipe out the deficit by 2002. The size of tax cuts, spending cuts and the president's request for some new programmes have been the major divisions.
Republicans wanted bigger tax cuts and reductions in Medicare spending than Democrats.
The White House had boosted its Medicare spending reduction to $115 billion from $100 billion spread over five years.
